title: Minimal-support coordinates of a vector fixed by an endomorphism
statement: Let $R$ be a commutative ring, $F$ a free $R$-module [def-weil-pbc-free-module], $x\in F$ a nonzero element, and $\pi:F\to F$ an $R$-linear endomorphism with $\pi(x)=x$. There exist a basis $\mathcal B$ of $F$, an integer $n\ge1$, distinct $e_1,\ldots,e_n\in\mathcal B$, and nonzero $a_1,\ldots,a_n\in R$ such that $x=\sum_{i=1}^n a_i e_i$, and $n$ is the least support cardinality of $x$ among all bases of $F$. For every $j$, there are no $c_i\in R$ with $a_j=\sum_{i\ne j}a_i c_i$. Put $T=\operatorname{span}_R(\mathcal B\setminus\{e_1,\ldots,e_n\})$ and $y_i=\pi(e_i)$. There exist $b_{ij}\in R$ and $t_i\in T$ such that $y_i=\sum_{j=1}^n b_{ij}e_j+t_i$ for every $i$, $x=\sum_{i=1}^n a_i y_i$, and $a_j=\sum_{i=1}^n a_i b_{ij}$ for every $j$. Here a support is the finite set of basis vectors with nonzero coefficient in the unique basis expansion. No finite-generation hypothesis is imposed on $F$.

source.place: Tag 0592, lemma-projective-freeness-criteria, proof first paragraph (minimal support and basis shear), second paragraph (projection coordinates), and last paragraph (comparison of coefficients)

proof.text: By [def-weil-pbc-free-module], every basis gives a unique finite expansion of $x$. The set of support cardinalities attained by bases is a nonempty subset of $\mathbb N$, so it has a least member $n$, attained by some basis $\mathcal B$. Since an empty expansion is zero and $x\ne0$, $n\ge1$. Enumerate this support as distinct $e_1,\ldots,e_n$, with its nonzero coefficients $a_1,\ldots,a_n$. Then $x=\sum_{i=1}^n a_i e_i$.

source.place: Tag 0592, lemma-projective-freeness-criteria, proof first paragraph: choose a basis with a minimal number of terms

proof.text:
Fix $j$ and suppose $a_j=\sum_{i
e j}a_i c_i$. Replace $e_i$ by $e_i\prime=e_i+c_i e_j$ for $1\le i\le n$, $i
e j$, and fix $e_j$ and every vector of $\mathcal B$ outside this finite list. This family is a basis by the unique-expansion definition [def-weil-pbc-free-module]: an old expansion with coefficients $d_e$ has new coefficients $d_{e_i}$ at $e_i\prime$ for $i
e j$, $d_{e_j}-\sum_{i
e j}d_{e_i}c_i$ at $e_j$, and unchanged coefficients elsewhere. Conversely, the old $e_j$-coefficient is the new $e_j$-coefficient plus $\sum_{i
e j}d_{e_i}c_i$; all other coefficients are unchanged. These mutually inverse formulas preserve finite support and give existence and uniqueness of each new expansion.

source.place: Tag 0592, lemma-projective-freeness-criteria, proof first paragraph: the basis shear, with the inverse coefficient formula written out

proof.text: In this new basis the coefficient of $e_j$ in $x$ is $a_j-\sum_{i\ne j}a_i c_i=0$, and the only remaining nonzero coefficients are the $a_i$ at $e_i\prime$, $i\ne j$. Its support thus has $n-1$ elements, contradicting minimality of $n$. Therefore no such $c_i$ exist, for every $j$. This uses only the expansion uniqueness in [def-weil-pbc-free-module].

source.place: Tag 0592, lemma-projective-freeness-criteria, proof first paragraph: the shear shortens the expression

proof.text: Keep the original minimizing basis. For each $i$, expand $y_i=\pi(e_i)$ uniquely in $\mathcal B$ using [def-weil-pbc-free-module]. Let $b_{ij}$ be its $e_j$-coefficient and let $t_i$ be the finite sum of its terms outside $\{e_1,\ldots,e_n\}$. By the definition of $T$ as their span, $t_i\in T$ and $y_i=\sum_{j=1}^n b_{ij}e_j+t_i$. Linearity and the hypothesis $\pi(x)=x$ give $\sum_{i=1}^n a_i y_i=\pi(\sum_{i=1}^n a_i e_i)=\pi(x)=x$.

source.place: Tag 0592, lemma-projective-freeness-criteria, proof second paragraph: coordinates of the projected vectors and the equality expressing x

proof.text: Every $t_i$ has zero $e_j$-coefficient for $1\le j\le n$. Substitute the expansions from the preceding step into $x=\sum_i a_i y_i$ and distribute the finite sums. Its $e_j$-coefficient is $\sum_{i=1}^n a_i b_{ij}$, while the original expansion has coefficient $a_j$. Uniqueness in [def-weil-pbc-free-module] gives $a_j=\sum_{i=1}^n a_i b_{ij}$ for each $j$. All sums used are finite even when $\mathcal B$ is infinite.
